books.section: Topic 9.5 Migration and Immigration, 1980 to the Present
Prosperity and a New World Order (1988–2000)

options.misconception: After 1965, most legal immigrants came from Latin America and Asia, not Europe.
options.text: It came almost entirely from Europe, as it had before the 1965 act

options.misconception: The 2010s total of 10.3 million was more than double the 1970s total of 4.4 million.
options.text: It was smaller in total, because the border had been closed
It was far larger, and most newcomers came from Latin America and Asia

options.misconception: Family reunification remained the largest path to a green card in the 2010s.
options.text: It consisted only of refugees, with no family-based admissions

rationales.A: Background: the 1965 act ended the quotas that had favored Europe, and Europe's share kept falling.
rationales.B: The table shows growth, from 4.4 million to 10.3 million, not a smaller total.
rationales.C: The decade total more than doubled, from 4.4 million to 10.3 million. Background: the 1965 act had shifted the main sources from Europe to Latin America and Asia, and that pattern held through the 2010s.
rationales.D: Background: family reunification, not refugee admissions, was the largest route to legal status.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the two decades in the table: 4.4 million in the 1970s, 10.3 million in the 2010s.
2. The size difference is the clearest change, so any choice saying it shrank is out.
3. Add the source shift. Background: after 1965, most newcomers came from Latin America and Asia, not Europe.
4. Refugees alone cannot explain the totals. Background: family admissions were larger.
Remember: compare both size and source when a question asks how two eras differ.

stem: Compared with the 1970s, legal immigration in the 2010s differed most clearly in which way?

stimulus.source_note: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, Table 1 (public data).
stimulus.text:
| Decade | People gaining lawful permanent resident status |
| 1971–1980 | 4.4 million |
| 1981–1990 | 7.3 million |
| 1991–2000 | 9.1 million |
| 2001–2010 | 10.5 million |
| 2011–2020 | 10.3 million |

Source: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, Table 1. Simplified for this test.
